newsitem.title: USA: U.S. economy slowed more than thought in third quarter.
newsitem.headline: U.S. economy slowed more than thought in third quarter.

text.p: Weak consumer spending and reduced production for inventories braked the economy's expansion more sharply during the third quarter than previously thought, the Commerce Department said Wednesday.
The nation's gross domestic product expanded at a revised 2 percent annual rate in the three months from July through September instead of 2.2 percent as estimated a month ago.

That was less than half the hearty 4.7 percent pace of increase in national output posted during the second quarter. But it still exceeded Wall Street economists' forecasts of an even more abrupt slowdown in third-quarter GDP to a 1.7 percent rate.

"This is slightly higher (than Wall Street estimates) but it really doesn't change the assessment of what's happening in the economy," said Larry Chimerine, chief economist at the Economic Strategy Institute.
"I would call this close to a non-event," added Martin Mauro, senior economist at Merrill Lynch. "There were really no surprises."
GDP measures the value of all goods and services produced by workers and capital within U.S. borders.

Commerce cited several factors contributing to the downward revision in third-quarter GDP, including less inventory investment, fewer net exports to foreign markets and slacker consumer spending on costly durable goods like new cars.
A few components of GDP were revised up from a month ago. They included more vigorous business investment in new plants and production equipment and increased spending by state and local governments.

The inflation-sensitive U.S. Treasury market gained after the report was issued, with the benchmark 30-year bond up 20/32 of a point, or $6.25 per $1,000 face value, and its yield, which moves in the opposite direction, fell to 6.40 percent from 6.45 percent Tuesday.
The GDP figures, the widest available measure of national economic activity, will be finally revised one more time a month from now.
Many economists expect the third-quarter deceleration in GDP will be temporary and that growth will pick up in the closing three months this year.
A relatively strong holiday shopping season between Thanksgiving and Christmas is widely anticipated and early reports from retailers show that shopping picked up in September and October.

"We're still looking for fourth quarter GDP to be close to 4.0 percent," said Mauro. "The real question for the fourth quarter is, 'What are consumers going to do after the lackluster third quarter?'"

Commerce said consumer spending grew at a revised annual rate of $6.7 billion a year, or 0.6 percent, in the third quarter, compared with the second quarter's $38.5 billion, or 3.4 percent. A month ago it said spending grew even more weakly, at a $5.2 billion rate, or 0.4 percent.
That was the weakest pace for consumer spending in nearly five years, since it contracted at a 1 percent rate in the fourth quarter of 1991.

"The deceleration in third-quarter GDP growth -- that is, the smaller increase in the third quarter than in the second quarter -- was more than accounted for by a sharp deceleration in personal consumption expenditures and by downturns in government, in residential investment and in exports," the department said.

Businesses increased inventories at a $32.8 billion annual rate in the third quarter instead of $39.6 billion as estimated a month ago. That was stronger than the addition to stocks of unsold goods at a $7.1 billion rate during the second quarter, though less robust than previously estimated.

International trade was a weak spot as Commerce said it revised down its estimate of the value of foreign exports on the basis of additional data from August and September. Imports were even stronger than estimated earlier.

Two inflation measures in the GDP report pointed to muted price rises. The implicit price deflator advanced at a 1.6 percent annual rate in the third quarter, the same as estimated a month ago, and similarly, the fixed-weights measure of price changes was unrevised at a 1.9 percent rate of increase.
